standard.title: Creating Civic Descriptions, Explanations and Arguments
standard.description: create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms that reference evidence
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can present descriptions and explanations drawing on sources and using relevant terms and conventions (AC9HS6S07). The Y7 shift is to civics-specific communication — using discipline concepts and terms (rule of law, separation of powers, secular nation), referencing evidence, and developing argument as a distinct form.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms that reference evidence.

nodes.label: Using civics concepts and terms accurately
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use civics and citizenship concepts and terms accurately in descriptions and explanations, connecting terms to their meanings rather than using them superficially.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least three civics concepts or terms correctly in a description or explanation (e.g. 'rule of law', 'separation of powers', 'secular nation', 'federalism'), demonstrating understanding of what each term means.
nodes.typical_width: Use appropriate civics concepts and terms (including 'rule of law', 'separation of powers', 'secular nation', 'responsible government', 'federalism', 'active citizenship') accurately in descriptions and explanations; demonstrate that terms are used to communicate genuine understanding rather than as decoration.
wider: Explain the same civic concept using both formal disciplinary language and accessible everyday language, practising the ability to code-switch between registers
Analyse a student or media example to identify where civics terms are used correctly vs incorrectly or superficially, developing evaluative judgement about term use
Build a personalised civics glossary that defines terms in own words with example sentences, supporting fluent use in writing
nodes.hinge_reason: Accurate use of civics concepts is the foundation for creating arguments that reference evidence — students who misuse terms will produce descriptions and arguments that fail to communicate genuine civic understanding. This is the language precision gate for civic communication.

response_modes.reason: Accurate term use requires practice and feedback — students need to see their term use evaluated and corrected, not just to learn definitions. Invest in regular writing tasks that require terms to be used in context.

success_criteria: Use at least three civics concepts or terms correctly in a piece of writing about a civic topic
Demonstrate that terms are used to communicate genuine understanding (not superficially) by explaining what each term means in context

nodes.label: Developing evidence-referenced explanations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop explanations that use civics knowledge and research to present an authoritative position on an issue, referencing specific evidence.
nodes.minimum_width: Write an explanation of a civic issue or system that references at least one piece of specific evidence (e.g. a law, a statistic, an example) to support the explanation.
nodes.typical_width: Develop explanations using civic and citizenship knowledge or research that present an authoritative position; reference specific evidence (laws, data, examples, cases); connect evidence to explanation rather than listing facts alongside claims.
wider: Develop an explanation that integrates evidence from multiple source types (e.g. legislation + statistical data + expert report) and explains how the evidence sources support each other
Evaluate an explanation written by someone else to identify where evidence is well-integrated and where claims are unsubstantiated
Revise an explanation after receiving feedback on evidence use — practising the iterative writing process

response_modes.reason: Connecting evidence to claims (not just including evidence alongside claims) is a writing skill that requires practice and iterative feedback — students need to write, receive feedback, and revise to develop this skill.

success_criteria: Write an explanation that references at least one piece of specific evidence
Connect the evidence to the explanation — showing why the evidence supports the claim rather than just listing it

nodes.label: Constructing civic arguments
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct a civic argument — a structured claim with supporting evidence and reasoning — appropriate to the purpose and audience, using relevant concepts and terms.
nodes.minimum_width: Write a short argument (claim + at least two supporting points + evidence) on a civic topic, using at least two relevant civics terms and presenting ideas appropriate to the audience.
nodes.typical_width: Develop civic arguments using appropriate terms and concepts; present ideas appropriate to purpose and audience (e.g. digital material promoting democratic participation, a written case for constitutional change); structure arguments with a clear position, supporting points, evidence, and coherent reasoning.
wider: Develop an argument for a simulated civic context (e.g. a submission to a parliamentary committee, a speech for a school community forum) and adapt tone and structure to that specific audience and purpose
Compare two arguments taking opposing positions on the same civic issue, evaluating which is better supported and identifying the weaknesses in each
Develop a multi-modal civic communication (e.g. digital presentation promoting participation in democracy) that integrates text, evidence, and visual elements

response_modes.reason: Argument construction integrates accurate term use (N1), evidence referencing (N2), and knowledge of civic systems — the argument is the performance that draws on all previous capabilities and knowledge nodes.

success_criteria: Construct a structured civic argument with a clear claim, at least two supporting points, and referenced evidence
Use at least two civics concepts or terms accurately and present ideas appropriate to the intended audience
